articles.title: Largely peaceful marches across France as workers stage strike, some police clashes reported
articles.summary: Some protesters clashed with police in Paris and Lyon on Thursday during largely peaceful nationwide demonstrations and a one-day strike by some public sector workers in a renewed challenge to…

image.caption: A man holds a French flag near fire in Lyon, France, as demonstrators attend a nationwide day of strikes and protests on Thursday over wages, the cost of living and public services, called by French labour unions and joined by high school and university students calling for better education conditio

blocks.text: World·Photos

Some protesters clashed with police in Paris and Lyon on Thursday during largely peaceful nationwide demonstrations and a one-day strike by some public sector workers in a renewed challenge to President Emmanuel Macron.
Protests come after weeks of demonstrations over living costs, public services and education

Some protesters clashed with police in Paris and Lyon on Thursday during largely peaceful nationwide demonstrations and a one-day strike by some public sector workers in a renewed challenge to French President Emmanuel Macron.

The protests were attended by several high-profile politicians, including presidential candidates Jean-Luc Mélenchon and Raphael Glucksmann. The protests follow demonstrations over living costs, public services and education that have triggered the worst civil unrest France has seen in years.
The Interior Ministry said 270,000 people had participated in protests around the country so far, excluding Paris, where the main demonstration started in the afternoon.

"This country needs justice," Glucksmann told reporters at the start of the Paris march. "We are going to bring the French people back together. We are going to restore public services; we will do ... the opposite of what's taken place in the past 10 years."
Riot police in Lyon detain protesters during a demonstration for higher wages and in support of the high school protest movement on Thursday. (Laurent Cipriani/The Associated Press)

In Paris, the mood was festive at the start, featuring a diverse group of participants singing La Marseillaise and some carnival-like floats. The Eiffel Tower was shut by the one-day strike, which was joined by some energy workers and teachers, but there were no major disruptions to transport.
But about two hours in, some of the people at the front of the march clashed with police, who fired tear gas.

In Lyon, riot police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters, some of whom were seen shouting anti-police slogans and dressed all in black, with face coverings. The Interior Ministry said the police there had been confronted by several hundred hardcore protesters and that the violence had been contained, although tensions remained high.
Students attend a demonstration in Paris on Thursday demanding more education funding in Paris. (Thibault Camus/The Associated Press)

The unrest comes only five months before a presidential election, which could pit far-right candidate Marine Le Pen against hard-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon in a second-round runoff. Macron, who is serving his second term and is unpopular, cannot run again.
"There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services," said Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris demonstration.
"I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers."
School ablaze after fireworks are hurled

The Interior Ministry said people throwing fireworks had caused a fire at a high school near the city of Toulouse in the southwest on Thursday morning, forcing pupils and staff to evacuate the building while firefighters doused the flames.
"This criminal behavior is an absolute scandal," said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on X.
French high school students and other demonstrators had earlier faced off against riot police in Paris as they blocked a street with rubbish bins on Thursday morning.
A protester dressed as the superhero Deadpool rides a toy unicorn during the Thursday demonstration in Lyon. (Laurent Cipriani/The Associated Press)
While the demonstrations in Lyon and other cities, including Marseille and Nantes, began in the morning, the main protest in Paris was only scheduled to start at 2 p.m. local time,.
The Eiffel Tower was shut on Thursday because of the strike.

"The government tried to block the demonstrations. The demonstrations are bigger than ever," Sophie Binet, head of the CGT trade union, told reporters. She estimated that some 250,000 people were demonstrating across France.
"High school students, pensioners, students, workers, all together. Unity wins," read one banner at the protest in Lyon.
Police deploy in large numbers
"Our pay has not kept up with inflation," said Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter who was joining the protest in Paris.

"What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced," he said, referring to wildfires caused earlier this year by intense heat waves.

Authorities had sought to lower tensions after riots and looting on Oct. 17 caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops and public buildings across the country and fuelling criticism of Macron's handling of the crisis.
A car burns during a demonstration in Lyon. (Laurent Cipriani/The Associated Press)
Around 70,000 police were on duty nationwide, a comparable figure to recent weekends. The French government has defended police tactics while saying any abuses would be investigated.
The Education Ministry said just over 15 per cent of French teaching staff had joined the strike.
Protests drawn into election campaigning

The movement began in September with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris and spread nationwide. It drew students demanding more education funding and workers seeking better pensions and help with soaring fuel prices and other costs.

The rallies come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political parties seeking to capitalize on the movement. Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite to win.
Tens of thousands march in France protests before police respond with tear gas and water cannons
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Russell Brand convicted of rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: British comedian and actor Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault linked to allegations dating back more than 20 years. He was acquitted of two…

image.caption: British actor and comedian Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London with his wife, Laura Brand, on Thursday. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Breaking

British comedian and actor Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault linked to allegations dating back more than 20 years. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Judge says actor will receive prison sentence
British comedian and actor Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would receive a prison term when he is sentenced on Monday. He was taken into custody.
A prosecutor said Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator."
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life, but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
A jury of eight men and four women in London's Southwark Crown Court deliberated for more than eight hours over two days.

Known for risqué standup routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

items: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at rape and sex assault trial
Russell Brand blocked from making money off YouTube

blocks.text: In recent years, he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.
His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defence, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

articles.title: A bitter end for Ronaldo - the icon who transformed Portugal
articles.summary: As Cristiano Ronaldo retires from international football, Guillem Balague looks at why and what is next for the Portugal legend.

blocks.text: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.
The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.

The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.

It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.
His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.
A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.

Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.
So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.
Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.
When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.

He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.

The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.

A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.
It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.

Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.

In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.

That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad. He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.

Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.

The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.
In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.
Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.
Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.

The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.
Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.

After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.
At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.
In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.
Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.
And Eder did.

But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.
His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.
When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.
That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.

Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.
No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.

Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.
Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.
After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.
In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.
After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.
Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.
The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.
Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

articles.title: Alex Eala edges Czech foe in thriller, nabs Hong Kong Open quarterfinal spot
articles.summary: World No. 17 Alex Eala completes a second-set comeback against steely Czech teen challenger Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals

blocks.text: POWER. Filipina tennis ace Alex Eala in action at the 2026 Hong Kong Open.
HONG KONG OPEN
World No. 17 Alex Eala completes a second-set comeback against steely Czech teen challenger Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals

MANILA, Philippines – Filipina tennis superstar Alex Eala brushed off the threat of an extended match in the clutch, eking out a thrilling 6-4, 7-6(7) straight-setter against Czech rival Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals on Thursday, November 5.
Down 5-3 in the second set after relentless back-and-forth action, Eala ignited the comeback fire with a love game to inch within 5-4, before completing a three-game turnaround to land at a 6-5 lead.
Valentova, however, stopped the bleeding in time to force the tiebreaker, 6-6.

Just as it looked like the 21-year-old Eala had her foe dead in the water with a 5-0 blitz in the race-to-seven finale, Valentova dug herself out with a scorching 6-1 rally of her own to set up yet another nail-biting finish for the Filipina sensation.
After four match points, Eala got the final break she needed on the serve, scoring the last two points to seal the deal and deny a valiant challenge from the world No. 85 Valentova.

“It was really, really tough. I think Tereza played incredibly, and we were able to bring the match to a really high level, and I think that was reflected on the scores,” Eala said after the match. “Really happy with that win, I think I escaped by a little bit.”

With the win, Eala also solved a yearlong puzzle featuring Valentova, as the Czech star swept the Filipina in their two previous meetings: a 6-1, 6-2 demolition in the 2025 Japan Open Round of 32 and a 7-6(6), 6-1 pullaway in the 2026 Qatar Open Round of 64.
“Of course, the previous two meetings [against her] were super difficult, so I knew it was going to be a tough battle,” Eala added. “I just tried to be better than the previous time we met.”
Eala faces another quick turnaround as world No. 81 Antonia Ruzic of Croatia awaits on the other side of the quarterfinal equation on Friday, November 6, around 7:40 pm. – Rappler.com

Is Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa hiding in Mindanao? Law enforcement agencies, unfortunately, have different answers.

The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) believes the senator is being protected by a “powerful armed group” in the Southern Philippines. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), meanwhile, says it cannot confirm his whereabouts.
“I cannot tell [if he’s in Mindanao] but we have a strong belief that he is still in the Philippines,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said on Thursday, November 5. “Though that’s still a possibility.”

Dela Rosa has remained out of public view since May, following the issuance of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant against him over his alleged role in the Duterte administration’s bloody drug war.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla previously said he received information that the legislator was being protected by an armed group in Mindanao. He also warned that a forced arrest could cost “10,000” lives, explaining why he would rather negotiate the senator’s surrender.
Remulla did not identify the alleged armed group, but the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) was quick to distance itself from the speculation.

The interior chief also gave Dela Rosa a one-week deadline to surrender, and offered a P50-million bounty for his arrest. After the deadline lapsed, the Philippine National Police (PNP) launched an intensified manhunt operation for their former chief.

“The NBI may soon launch some operations to eliminate the areas that we will identify based on the intelligence reports…With the information we are getting, there is a great chance for his arrest,” Matibag said.
Asked whether the senator would be arrested by Christmas, Matibag replied: “We hope so.”

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued a warrant against Dela Rosa in November last year due to his role in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. He was Duterte’s first police chief who implemented the bloody anti-drug campaign, which human rights organizations said, took the lives of as many as 30,000 people.

The ICC named him a co-perpetrator in the case. It added that those involved “controlled a structure of power” which enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out drug war killings.

Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Lakas ng Bayan, Dela Rosa’s political party, has appealed to the Supreme Court for a swift resolution of Dela Rosa’s case. The senator’s camp also urged the High Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an ICC warrant of arrest against him.

With Dela Rosa still nowhere to be found, Malacañang has challenged the PNP leadership to ensure his arrest, putting pressure on the police force once led by the senator. Will they heed his call or remain loyal to their ex-PNP chief? – with reports by Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

articles.title: One Nation asks donors at $3,000-a-head Sydney fundraiser to accept ‘non-disclosure agreement’
articles.summary:
Transparency experts raise concerns about plans to use NDA to gag attendees at event featuring Pauline Hanson in lead-up to NSW election

  • Get our

blocks.text: One Nation is attempting to gag donors from ever revealing details of discussions at an invite-only, cocktail-dress fundraiser with the party’s senior leadership team, in a move described as a “worrying precedent” for democracy.
Invitations to the “very special evening” at an undisclosed central Sydney venue next Thursday show donors will be charged $3,000 for a “private and very discrete” four-hour event.

Donors have been told they’ll meeting with Pauline Hanson; One Nation’s national director, James Ashby; federal MP Barnaby Joyce; the federal party’s chief of staff, Chris Taylor; and its New South Wales leader, Mike Newman.

But unlike at other One Nation fundraisers – including a $2,000 invite-only event in Melbourne in September – this time donors have been asked to abide by a “non-disclosure agreement” preventing them from disclosing the identities of any attendees. They are also stopped from sharing the nature of any discussions at the event, which is reportedly set to feature a “cocktail and canapé service throughout the evening as the sun sets” and a live auction.

“Do not disclose information about what occurs at the event, including conversations, activities, photographs, video or other details obtained through attending,” says the agreement, contained in an invitation seen by Guardian Australia.
“Do not provide information, photographs, recordings or comments about the event to journalists, media organisations, bloggers or other publishers.”
The NDA states that these obligations “continue after the event has concluded”.

These type of fundraising dinners are common and frequently organised by Labor and Liberal parties. But senior sources from both major parties involved in running such events say the use of non-disclosure agreements is unprecedented.

Transparency International Australia’s chief executive, Clancy Moore, has been a long-term critic of closed-door fundraising dinners and believes they offer “cash for access”. He said the use of non-disclosure agreements was a worrying new step.
“Charging guests for a political fundraiser and requiring them to keep quiet about it raises serious questions about transparency ahead of an important state election,” Moore said.

“Voters deserve to know whether any political commitments are being made behind closed doors to paying guests. A non-disclosure agreement should never be used to shield political fundraising from public scrutiny.”
Christian Slattery, a senior campaigner at the Australian Democracy Network, said Australians were “rightly suspicious of exclusive cash-for-access events”.
“Slapping an NDA on a political fundraiser sets a worrying precedent. Democracy thrives in the sunlight,” Slattery said.
One Nation has disclosed $5,000 in reportable donations so far in 2026-27, across three donations for a fundraising dinner with Joyce, according to disclosures with the NSW Electoral Commission.
In that time, disclosures indicate the NSW Labor party has raised $286,200 in total reportable donations, while the NSW Liberals have raised $95,900.
after newsletter promotion
The individual threshold for a reportable donation in New South Wales is $1,000.
Major donations drive
A now-defunct webpage containing details of Thursday’s event had stated that registered attendees would receive a text message with its location just an hour before the start time.
In early September, the address of a three-course fundraising lunch with Hanson in Melbourne was leaked to the media, leading to journalists photographing donors as they entered the venue.
Other high-profile fundraisers in the state have been targeted by protesters, leading to clashes with One Nation supporters and a heavy police presence.

One Nation has also required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media or revealing confidential information obtained during the process.

The fundraiser comes amid a major donations drive by the party in NSW, where it was polling at 25% of the first-preference vote, ahead of the Coalition on 24% and behind Labor on 29%, according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in September. Polling conducted internally by Labor suggests One Nation could pick up more than 20 seats in the state’s lower house.
Newman and Joyce hosted several publicly advertised, small-ticket dinners and forums in October, with more events planned in November.
One Nation was contacted for comment.

articles.title: Australians are yet to see the benefits of AI and datacentres – and US midterms show they could be political kryptonite
articles.summary:
Albanese should tread carefully as he struggles to make case for how the new technology will benefit ordinary voters

  • Get our

blocks.text: When will Australia see the benefits of the AI and datacentre boom? So far, all we’ve seen is the possibility of changes to copyright which would hurt Australian creatives, special rules about power and water use, and the threat of mass displacement or replacement of workers, with the trade-off being a mere 10% chance of human extinction.
Now add the Reserve Bank’s assessment this week that datacentres were part of growing “inflationary pressures” when lifting interest rates to an 18-year high.

Warnings about looming negatives have been coming for months, but even the RBA has no idea when to expect the positives. And, as the results of the US midterms show us, datacentres are becoming political kryptonite for voters not sold on the AI boom, meaning the Albanese government should tread carefully.

As Labor mulls its long-awaited plan to attract AI investment, this week’s RBA decision demands politicians better explain what the benefits of this rollout will be, and why it is worth the (hopefully short-term) pain. It also requires the government to consider other inflation responses, beyond the RBA.
The governor, Michele Bullock, warned “some pain now will prevent even worse pain” in the future. But why should ordinary workers endure pain that is not of their own making?

Some of the richest companies in the world are helping heat the economy to such an extent that Bullock flagged it in her opening remarks, just moments after pointing to global oil prices, low productivity and expectations of prolonged inflation.

“Parts of demand have also been stronger than expected. In particular, investment has been much stronger than expected, including due to datacentre-related investment. This has added to inflationary pressures by adding to demand at a time when the domestic economy is already capacity constrained,” Bullock said.
The RBA’s statement of monetary policy highlighted that “AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods” in its second paragraph.
But asked when AI would start having a “positive impact on inflation”, Bullock shrugged “your guess is as good as mine”.
She said “if productivity improves dramatically because of AI” – “if”, not “when” – then we would see faster growth, but also warned it could increase the “neutral interest rate”.
“So if people think that productivity improvements will help to lower inflation and keep interest rates low, that’s not necessarily the case,” Bullock said.
Even the nation’s chief economic wonk is hazy on when the benefits start flowing.

These aren’t nimby arguments against datacentres or luddite concerns about technological growth; there are serious economic questions to be considered here, and social ones already being examined worldwide.
Deloitte Access Economics on Thursday reported Australia’s $1.39tn investment pipeline included 37 datacentres worth $141bn – a 36% increase in a year.

Deloitte director, Sheraan Underwood, said the datacentre boom was “competing directly with housing and infrastructure for workers and materials”, and that Australia had “less room to absorb” the investment surge thanks to high inflation.

Deloitte reported “the economic dividend may take time”, predicting “substantial” construction gains but that the “direct economic payoff” wouldn’t be as big. The technology fit-out is largely imported goods and few workers are needed to actually staff the facilities.
after newsletter promotion

Of course the datacentre boom will support AI takeup, greater automation and productivity, but Deloitte warned: “Construction demand and inflation pressures are arriving now, while the productivity dividend may come much later.”

In the wake of RBA warnings about demand, much media focus has naturally turned to government spending. Press gallery pundits have zeroed in, particularly, on green subsidies and home batteries; the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, blasted a “blowout” from a budgeted $2.3bn to $8.5bn.
That’s $6.2bn more than budgeted. Or, in another way, 4% of the total $141bn datacentre investment.
Or 16% of the growth in datacentre investment in just one year.

Economics and finance, like politics, is a series of choices. If everything is on the table for savings, as Labor has said, shouldn’t we consider the benefits of untrammelled investment in AI factories before we start slashing social programs achieving good?

This week’s datacentre backlash in the United States is instructive. Politico recently reported polling showing half of Americans oppose datacentres near their homes; NBC exit polls found 56% of voters said AI and datacentres were “crucial” or “major” factors in the midterms. Datacentres were also literally on the ballot in dozens of towns, with public votes overwhelmingly won by proposals to restrict construction, according to vote trackers.
The Australian backlash is much smaller, but growing. Community groups are organising and protesting. Labor should not overlook bubbling voter unease.

So what to do instead? Beyond leaving it to the “blunt instrument” of monetary policy for the RBA to smash the economy, there are other options Labor could consider. They are novel, but the times demand novel solutions.

Senator David Pocock has proposed a Senate committee to investigate “alternatives” to monetary policy, suggesting options including “temporary, progressive” changes to income tax or superannuation. Independent economist Saul Eslake has said a small rise in superannuation rates, from even 12 to 13%, would take some money out of workers’ pockets and help curb spending. Pocock, again, suggested taxes on windfall profits and gas exports to take more cash out of the economy.

Of course we need new AI and datacentre investment, particularly as the government looks for a magic bullet to end stagnant productivity. But the government has so far struggled to make the case for how this new technology will benefit ordinary Australians, who are left with a feeling of uncertainty and a hole in their back pocket.

articles.title: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war
articles.summary:
Dismissals follow Houthi victories and pressure from southern Yemenis for more power

The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt…

blocks.text: The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.

A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
Reuters reported on Monday that Houthi forces were only about 37 miles (60km) from Aden, the nominal seat of the UN-recognised government.
A burst of government dismissals and appointments reflects military reverses and possibly a perceived need to be more sensitive to the demands of southern Yemenis.

Between 1967 and 1990, the country was divided in two, and there is a strong movement built around the banned Southern Transitional Council (STC) seeking to revert to that division, or create a more federated country.
The government has become dependent on southern troops to fend off Houthi advances, but these forces insist they will fight only to defend land inside former South Yemen.

Fresh claims were also aired this week that STC leaders were coerced by the Saudis into dissolving the organisation against their will. The growing criticism of Saudi Arabia from STC officials in the media reflects their confidence that if the north is lost to the Houthis, the Saudis will have to let the STC operate openly. Not all southern separatists support the STC, an organisation that overreached itself in January, making it easier for the Saudi leadership to defer decisions on the southern question.

Some of the most senior figures in the UN-backed government are largely based in hotels in Riyadh rather than operating permanently from inside Yemen and the government is dependent on Saudi money to pay salaries. Critics say the administration has become a “hotel government”.

Earlier this week, its ruling executive – the presidential leadership council – met for the first time in months in Riyadh, where it addressed the loss of swathes of territory to the Houthis along Yemen’s west coast. Since then, the fighting has moved into the mountains around Taiz.

In an attempt to rebalance the north-south divide in his government, President Rashad al-Alimi sacked the long-serving information minister, Muammar al-Eryani, replacing him with Prof Salem al-Awlaki, previously a minister for the civil service and a spokesperson for the STC from 2017 to 2019. Alimi chose two other southerners as ministers for local administration and the civil service and appointed new leaders for the civil aviation authority, the ports of Aden and the ministry of transport.

blocks.caption: Camels in besieged Taiz, which is the third largest city in Yemen. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters

blocks.text: He also sacked Yusuf al-Sharaji, the military figure responsible for the Taiz front and Abu Bakr al-Jabouli, a brigadier responsible for the Tor al-Baha axis. Widespread accusations had been made about al-Sharaji’s failure to manage operations, resulting in the fall of several areas and districts to the Houthis.
The task of lifting the siege of Taiz and coordinating forces has been handed to Maj Gen Rashad al-Yousfi, a career officer.

Part of the difficulty is the tension between the different forces fighting on the government’s side. It has been claimed that Abu Zara’a, the leader of the Southern Giants, has fallen out with the Homeland Shield Forces, which are funded by Saudi Arabia and affiliated with Abdulrahman al-Lahji.

The Homeland Shield experienced heavy losses, leading al-Lahji to file an official report accusing Abu Zara’a of treason, and warning that the situation in Dhubab, close to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, had become extremely dangerous for the government. Repeated claims that control of the strait had been wrested back from the Houthis were contradicted by the evidence.

articles.title: What does Trump's midterm elections loss mean for strained US-India ties?
articles.summary: Donald Trump's electoral setback might give New Delhi and Washington space to reset relations, but there is no guarantee that the US will actually change its approach to India.

image.caption: While the US and India remain engaged in dialogue, the relationship between them has grown tenseImage: Nathan Howard/REUTERS

blocks.text: With the US Democrats scoring a resounding midterm victory and taking control of both chambers of Congress, the Republican administration led by Donald Trump is set for a new level of scrutiny until the end of Trump's term.

Trump is likely to face pushback on his controversial foreign policy, which saw the US alienate most of its allies and get entangled in yet another unpopular war in the Middle East. At the same time, the Trump administration has also taken a slew of less conspicuous but still highly controversial moves on the global stage, including a series of confrontations with India.

The ties between New Delhi and Washington are still strained by a stalled trade agreement, restrictions on immigration, and disagreement over India buying Russian oil and weapons, despite the US granting an oil ban waiver in March 2026 and Trump waving some of the Russia sanctions in October.
And while the new US Congress can choose to pressure Trump over issues such as tariffs and immigration, the president still wields significant authority on foreign policy.
Congress likely to look into Trump's trade restrictions

The immediate test for Trump's India policy is trade. India and the US have yet to formalize the interim framework discussed by Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in February, with the two nations still at odds over market access and other trade commitments.
US top diplomat Marco Rubio in India to renew strained ties
Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, founder of the Mantraya Institute of Strategic Studies, expects the new Congress to apply "increased scrutiny of protectionist measures" pushed by the Trump administration.
The US lawmakers could push for "stronger trade oversight and clearer standards for environmental and labor issues," she told DW.
For India, whose largest export market is the US, this could offer some breathing room.
She also emphasized that "the fundamental pillars of the India-US strategic partnership are expected to remain strong" and "the long-term goal of deepening economic ties is likely to continue."
'The president is not rational'

Immigration presents a different challenge. The administration's tightening of H-1B visa rules, including imposing a $100,000 (€88,761) payment for certain new petitions, has alarmed Indian professionals and tech companies that rely on the visa program to secure jobs in the US.
A Democratic majority could increase scrutiny on that issue as well, but would not automatically reverse measures introduced by Trump's executive action.
"Both parties have bigger issues to grapple with," said Rajkrishna Iyer, a California-licensed immigration lawyer. "For the last 25-plus years, Congress has done nothing for immigration," he added.
What defeat in US midterm elections could mean for Trump
Iyer believes that legal immigration itself is not a major priority for voters. Nevertheless, he sees the midterms' result as a message to Trump about his immigration policies.
"A rational president would not spend time imposing further restrictions on legal immigration. But as we know, the president is not rational," Iyer said.
The immigration lawyer believes that new, steep fee for some H-1B applications will be challenged in court.
"Most likely, the new rules will not come into effect. And if they do, federal courts are likely to strike them down because the fees are not reasonable," said Iyer.

While the executive branch of government can raise fees to reflect administrative costs and inflation, Iyer argues that charges of this magnitude could deter people from pursuing legal immigration. "Only Congress can pass such legislation," he said.
US still wants less dependence on Russia

The new balance of power in Washington could also trigger a new geopolitical reshuffle and a change of course on Russia. However, it is unclear if the Democrat-dominated Congress will force any changes in the dispute between New Delhi and Washington over India's purchasing Russian energy. During a congressional vote on Russian sanctions in September, a substantial number of Democrats joined Republican lawmakers to endorse trade restrictions against Moscow.
When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations

"Regarding Russian oil, the administration is likely to maintain its preference for reducing dependence on Moscow, but it will approach this issue with diplomatic caution to avoid straining relations with New Delhi," D'Souza says.
India angry over US supplying Pakistan with weapons
The war in Iran adds another dimension. Any new escalation could affect energy exports from the Middle East and make India more vulnerable due to its need for high oil imports.
But Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the US and Israel, urges cautions when discussing the future of US policy in the Middle East.
"It may be facile to try and parse these results for their immediate impact on specific areas of foreign policy. Much will depend on how Trump reacts," Sarna told DW.
At the same time, Sarna expects Washington to become "a more contested place," with greater congressional pushback on issues that divide India and the US.
"If that injects some balance and stability and restores institutional linkages it's good for the long-term future of our relationship," he added.

Security cooperation is another stumbling block. New Delhi is still by far the biggest buyer of Russia's arms exports, which irritates Washington. At the same time, India has objected to US supplying weapons to Pakistan, including the $686 million sale of advanced military tech for Pakistan's F-16 jets.

"Washington's military support for Pakistan remains a complex issue. However, ongoing regional adjustments and US concerns about stability in the region will probably prevent any significant policy changes," said D'Souza.
How India has become Russia's trade lifeline
Trump could 'double down' on New Delhi policy
The broader question is whether the election produces a more predictable Washington or a more confrontational Donald Trump.
A weakened president could be more inclined to seek compromises at home. But Trump could also respond to congressional resistance by taking a harder line elsewhere.

"We hope the electoral setback will prompt Trump to undertake a more considered review of his earlier actions," Amitabh Mattoo, dean of the School of International Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told DW.
But he also warns that it too early to assess the implications for India-US relations.

"Rather than moderating his approach, the president could double down and adopt an even harder line towards New Delhi if he comes to believe that Indians, particularly sections of the diaspora, played a role, directly or indirectly, in his party's defeat."
Business as usual for US and India?

Harsh Pant of the Observer Research argues that the US president retains considerable leverage over foreign policy despite the Republican setback, and that the India-US partnership has traditionally enjoyed bipartisan support.
How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation?
"I don't think India will be one of those issues" on which the White House and Congress are likely to clash, Pant told DW.
But the experience of the past two years, he argues, reinforces the need for India to reduce its dependence on any single partner.

"The need for diversification of partnerships, the need to be self-reliant in certain critical sectors, the need to have alternative supply chains — all of those issues remain where they are. The US midterms do not really change the calculus," he says.

articles.title: Cardinal Advincula urges prayers amid El Niño's worsening heat impact
articles.summary: In a circular letter released Thursday, Advincula directed all parishes and communities under the Archdiocese of Manila to pray the Oratio Imperata ad Petendam Pluviam during Eucharistic celebrations.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 9:33pm
Manila Archbishop Jose Cardinal Advincula has called on the faithful to offer prayers as a very strong El Niño is expected to bring record-breaking heat.

In a circular letter released Thursday, Advincula directed all parishes and communities under the Archdiocese of Manila to pray the Oratio Imperata ad Petendam Pluviam during Eucharistic celebrations.
The Oratio Imperata ad Petendam Pluviam will be prayed after the Post-Communion Prayer starting Sunday, November 8, until notice of the lifting of this instruction.
"As we implore the Lord to grant us the gift of rain, let us be reminded of the power of united prayer," Advincula said.
"When we come together as one community of faith, we entrust our needs and concerns to God's loving providence, confident that He hears the prayer of His beloved people," he added.

Advincula also urged priests, catechists, religious educators and those engaging in Christian formation to "take this opportunity to deepen the faithful's understanding of our Christian responsibility to care for creation."
"Let us help our communities recognize that the natural world is not merely a resource to be consumed, but a precious gift entrusted by the Creator to our care and stewardship," he said.

According to PAGASA, the El Niño phenomenon from the latter part of 2026 to the first half of 2027 is expected to be record-breaking in terms of heat, with temperatures across the Philippines expected to rise by 2C.

“Most climate models predict that the ongoing El Niño will persist until the first quarter of 2027, with its peak expected before the end of 2026. And its associated impacts may continue through the first half of 2027,” PAGASA Climate Monitoring and Prediction Section Chief Ana Liza Solis said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces international retirement
articles.summary: 'If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it,' says Ronaldo

blocks.text: RONALDO. In this file photo from July 2026, Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo looks dejected after the match as Portugal are eliminated from the World Cup.
IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters/Jerome Miron
'If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it,' says Ronaldo

items: Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from the Portugal national team, concluding a 23-year international career during which he made 234 appearances and scored 146 goals.
He captained Portugal to significant victories, including the Euro 2016 and the Nations League titles in 2019 and 2025, and expressed gratitude to his family, teammates, and the Portuguese people.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Cristiano Ronaldo said on Thursday, November 5, he was retiring from the Portugal team, bringing the curtain down on one of the most illustrious international careers in the history of football.
The 41-year-old announced that he would ‘hand back the number 7 shirt’ after the November international break.
Ronaldo captained Portugal to their first major trophy at Euro 2016 and helped them win the 2019 and 2025 Nations Leagues.
“It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made only with the head. They are also made with the heart,” said Ronaldo.
“If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it.”
Ronaldo thanked his family, the Portuguese people, and the teammates, coaches, and staff he worked with over his 23-year career with the national team.
“Portugal will always be a part of me,” he captioned the announcement video.
Ronaldo has made 234 appearances for Portugal and scored 146 goals. He holds the all-time record for international appearances and for international goals.

His final international tournament appearance was at the 2026 World Cup, where he tried to win the one major trophy that has eluded him. Portugal exited in the last 16 with a 1-0 loss to eventual champions and Iberian rivals Spain.
Ronaldo did, however, join Argentina’s Lionel Messi as the only players to feature at six global tournaments, one of a host of international records set by the Al-Nassr forward.

Ronaldo left the Portugal camp at the end of September ahead of their Nations League match against Denmark without permission and did not return. He later cited broken promises from manager Jorge Jesus as the reason for his departure.
Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following Portugal’s 2-1 win.
After Ronaldo apologized and said he remained available for international selection, the Portuguese Football Federation suspended the forward for 30 days and fined him €255 ($287.16).

Portugal, who top Nations League Group A4, hosts second-placed Denmark on November 14 in Braga before visiting Wales in their final two group games, which will be Ronaldo’s final chances to add to his international statistics.
The Portuguese Football Federation released a statement after Ronaldo’s retirement announcement, expressing its profound and eternal gratitude for his services.
“More than an exceptional athlete, our captain was an inspiring leader, an example of dedication and the ultimate symbol of the soul of our National Team,” said the statement.
Ronaldo will leave the international stage as Portugal’s most successful player in terms of individual and team honors and has become a cultural reference point for the country around the world.

“I spent my life working to become the best player in the world. Today I realise that my greatest victory was having deserved the honor of representing the best country in the world,” said Ronaldo in his statement. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duterte at ICC: Expert report on 'systemic practice' of EJKs sought for admission
articles.summary: ICC prosecutors seek to include reports of three expert witnesses, one of whom states a “systemic practice” of extrajudicial killings during Rodrigo Duterte"s presidency..
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III and JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 8:35pm

THE HAGUE — In a latest filing to admit prior recorded statements and materials as evidence, International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors seek to include reports of three expert witnesses, one of whom states a “systemic practice” of extrajudicial killings during former President Rodrigo Duterte’s presidency.

In its eleventh Rule 68(3) application, released publicly on November 4, the Office of the Prosecutor stated that the expert reports of P-1162, P-1071, and P-1078 are “relevant, reliable, and probative”, and not prejudicial to Duterte’s rights.

One of the experts, identified in the filing as P-1162, analyzed fatality patterns in anti-drug operations and found that the scale of killings could not plausibly be explained by legitimate self-defense.

His analysis compared the number of suspects killed and wounded, police officers killed, and the number of anti-illegal drug operations. It also compared Philippine figures with national, regional and international data, with particular focus on Bulacan.

Prosecutors said that P-1162 noted that the ratios between suspects and police officers killed “provide a compelling evidentiary basis to conclude that a vast majority of these encounters were staged to mask targeted killings, representing a systemic practice of extrajudicial execution rather than legitimate law enforcement.”
Expert report: Duterte-era police killings “extreme and a statistical outlier”

In his expert report, P-1162 also described police use of deadly force during Duterte’s presidency as “extreme and a statistical outlier,” even when compared with “jurisdictions notorious for violent policing.”
P-1162’s addendum also compares Duterte-era deaths with baseline figures from the presidencies of Benigno Aquino III and Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
The expert found, the filing says, that the number of deaths under Duterte “significantly exceed the number that would be expected having regard to the respective baselines.”
The prosecution is seeking to introduce two datasets compiled by P-1162, materials supplied to him by prosecutors, other sources he relied on, and previous reports he authored.
Two academics called in as expert witnesses
Meanwhile, the prosecutors described P-1071 and P-1078 as “widely published and recognized” academics.

The two experts, also included on the ICC Registry’s List of Experts, have “extensive experience testifying as expert witnesses in litigation,” although their field of expertise and litigation experience are currently unknown in the public document.

The filing states that the joint expert report of P-1071 and P-1078 comprises associated materials, including items “letters of instruction”, as well as other undisclosed items provided for by the prosecution, which have been “directly reviewed, relied upon, and cited by” the two experts. The collection also has other materials collected and disclosed by the prosecution, but not provided to the two expert witnesses.

“The Joint Expert Report and its associated material will assist the Chamber in its determination of the truth,” the filing stated. Prosecutors are also asking the Chamber to allow P-1071 and P-1078 to appear for focused supplementary questioning on discrete parts and topics covered by the report.

The prosecution has requested an undisclosed number of hours, divided “as necessary,” for the supplementary examination of P-1071 and P-1078 to expedite the proceedings and allow time for questioning by Duterte’s defense, the Common Legal Representatives for Victims, and the Chamber.

This filing—the eleventh for Rule 68(3), and the latest to be released publicly—is the fourteenth overall in a series of Rule 68(2)(b) and Rule 68(3) applications made by the Office of the Prosecutor in its bid to shorten the proceedings of what are expected to be lengthy presentations during Duterte’s trial.
The former president will go on trial at the ICC for crimes against humanity on November 30. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Pioneering Jewish academy opens in Germany
articles.summary: A Jewish academy has opened its doors in Frankfurt. The Central Council of Jews in Germany, the country’s leading Jewish umbrella group, set up the project to combat hate and promote dialogue and…

image.caption: The new Jewish Academy of the Central Jews in Germany combines tradition and modernity Image: Michael Probst/REUTERS

blocks.text: The western city of Frankfurt was a very conscious choice of location for the new academy, which is the first of its kind in Germany. Frankfurt has traditionally been a hub of Jewish intellectual life, as well as being one of the most important centers of Jewish life in Germany today, alongside Berlin, Munich and Düsseldorf.

Less than a ten-minute walk from the city's biggest synagogue, the Jewish Academy is also within sight of the historic festival hall building on Frankfurt Trade Fair grounds where the Nazis herded Jewish men in 1938 and deported them to concentration camps.

It was also here that the Central Council of Jews in Germany was founded in 1950; Berlin serves as its headquarters today. Frankfurt is also home to the Central Welfare Board of Jews in Germany (ZWST) and a Jewish museum that opened in 1988.

But most significantly,Jewish thinkers have played a key role in Frankfurt's intellectual and academic history. The city's Jewish community contributed to the establishment of Goethe University in 1914.

Another important legacy is the Jewish Lehrhaus (house of study). Founded in 1920, it quickly gained prominence and is today associated with the philosopher Franz Rosenzweig (1886–1929). It was closed by the Nazis in 1938. The new academy sees itself in the tradition of Rosenzweig's Lehrhaus.
A place of education and dialogue
Speaking at the opening ceremony (November 2), Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, stressed: "We must combat hatred with education, education and more education."

blocks.caption: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier (second from right) was at the opening ceremony of the Jewish Academy Image: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP

blocks.text: Schuster said the institute was a "milestone” that represented the "Jewish community's determination to call Germany home." At the same time, he emphasized: "Jewish life in Germany is under greater threat than it has been since the crime against humanity that was the Shoah."
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier also underlined the need to reject antisemitism "outright and without reservation." He added that it must also be combated politically.

The federal president said the murder of six million Jews in the Holocaust had also targeted the Jewish world of learning and knowledge. He specifically honored Rosenzweig's legacy: "This place of knowledge and dialogue was a source of hope, something exciting and something new."
A bridge between tradition and modernity, as well as academia and the general public
The Jewish Academy combines traditional features of a 110-year-old turn-of-the-century German villa with a four-story modern structure, bringing together old and new, history and modernity.
"We see ourselves as a place where the past, present and future are all explored in equal measure," Sabena Donath, the institution's director, told DW.
Donath and her co-director, Doron Kiesel, view the academy as "a bridge between academia and the general public" and as "a home for scholars and a home for those who ask questions."

blocks.caption: Doron Kiesel and Sabena Donath are the co-directors of the new institutionImage: Rafael Herlich

blocks.text: Donath said the aim was to put the focus on topics related to the philosophy of religion and ethics, as well as on topical debates concerning contemporary Jewish life.
The program aims to reflect the many facets of Jewish life and the diverse forms of Judaism.
Kiesel told DW: "We want to show how Jews live today and how heterogeneous Jewish life is. And that it is completely wrong to speak of 'the' Jews or 'the' Jewish way of thinking."

Ahead of the opening, the president of the Central Council of Jews also named interfaith dialogue as one of the institution's topics, and in an interview with the German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine, Schuster expressed the hope that the academy would bring into the public sphere "Jewish themes besides the topic of antisemitism and Jewish persecution.”

But these issues will also be on the agenda. "We have,” said Kiesel, "a problem in this country that antisemitism is concealed behind numerous topics, but keeps on resurfacing, sometimes more evidently, sometime more subtly.”
Germany's Jews and antisemitism: A complex reality

The project grew out of an initiative from the former head of the Central Council Dieter Graumann, who encouraged the setting up of an educational department in 2012. Its work was shaped by the directors of the new institution.
Security measures push up price tab

A mezuzah — a small capsule containing verses from the Torah intended to serve as a reminder of God's commandments — is affixed to the entrance of the academy. Security measures are also an integral part of this new building.

"It is a bitter reality that Jewish institutions must be guarded," said Donath. The academy is being protected just as Jewish schools and synagogues must be protected. "For us, this is a sad reality of everyday life."

The construction costs of around €40 million ($45 million) — about half of which was covered by the Central Council of Jews and half by the federal and state governments — ended up being significantly higher than calculated at the groundbreaking in 2021, partly due to the structural security measures.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
articles.summary: The announcement by the footballing legend comes just weeks after a public spat with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo appeared in the 2026 World Cup at the age of 41Image: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.
"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.
"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world."

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals – making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.
Decision made with 'head and heart'
He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.
"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.
"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it."
He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.
'The greatest of all time'
The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7."
"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!"

blocks.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo captained Portugal to the 2016 Euros titleImage: Reuters/C. Platiau

blocks.text: The FPF said it intended to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."
Training camp walkout

While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

Ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.
Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career – with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

MANILA, Philippines – World No. 1 pickleball player Anna Leigh Waters makes a quick return to the Philippines.

Following a well-received debut tour in Manila last October, Waters will next grace the legendary Araneta Coliseum on December 9 with a series of world-class exhibitions and other activities, while organizers have also promised musical performances with celebrity guests.

“The moment Anna Leigh Waters stepped onto Philippine soil last October, the clamor from fans and players was electric,” organizers shared in an official statement on Thursday, November 5. “We quickly realized that an ordinary venue simply wouldn’t suffice.

“Moving this showcase to the Smart Araneta Coliseum was an easy decision driven entirely by the overwhelming public demand. We want to ensure that as many fans as possible have the opportunity to witness the world’s greatest pickleball player in action, live.”

blocks.caption: How world No. 1 Anna Leigh Waters balances life and pickleball

blocks.text: General ticket sales for the event presented by wellness brand IAM Worldwide begin on Monday, November 9, following a limited exclusive sale period this Thursday, November 5.

“Pickleball is more than just a game to me. It’s speed, focus, and endurance, all in one. That’s why I am more than willing to support a community that values performance and wellness together,” the 19-year-old American sensation said in a video release.

“Let’s celebrate sports, health, and the power of staying strong together,” added the teenage prodigy, who has been the all-time women’s pickleball pro title record holder since October 2022 at age 15.

Waters has also been the undisputed pickleball pro title record holder since November 2025, after eclipsing doubles partner and men’s world No. 1 Ben Johns, and has since won an unprecedented 200th career title at the 2026 PPA Veolia Chicago Cup last October.

Passionate Filipino fans arrived in droves to meet the global face of pickleball in her last foray on Manila soil, as Waters joined packed crowds in various Taguig and Makati sports apparel stores last October 13 to 15.

Already part of TIME100’s Most Influential People in Sports, the young Waters also gamely shared her life success story to fans and media, and encouraged Filipino players to fully enjoy and embrace the process of the rising sport. – Rappler.com

articles.title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
articles.summary: The widow of ER creator Michael Crichton argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the 1990s series.

blocks.text: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled.
The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit.
Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.

A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.

Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained.
"We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.
It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.
But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.
The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.
ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.
The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.
Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.
Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.

But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series.
They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs".
Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.

After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".
But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim.
Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".

The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events.

Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."
Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

articles.title: North Korea tells EU to 'mind its own business' on human rights
articles.summary: North Korea's UN mission has lashed out at the European Union over a draft UN resolution. Pyongyang has said the West does not have a monopoly on human rights.

image.caption: Under Kim Jong Un's regime, North Korea is one of the most restrictive countries in the worldImage: KCNA/KNS/AFP

blocks.text: North Korea, responded European Union's draft United Nations resolution on human rights in the country by telling the bloc to "mind its own business," state media reported Thursday.
Pyongyang has long been accused by the UN and human rights advocates of committing human rights violations.
North Korea's UN mission said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency that the move was a "farce" and a "politically motivated provocation."
It said the resolution is "flagrantly distorting it's human rights policy," claiming that human rights are not "a monopoly of the West."
Referring to the protests in Europe, "Streets are filled with demonstrators from all walks of life demanding such elementary rights as the rights to existence," the North Korean mission said.
"The EU had better mind its own business, instead of hyping up the non-existent 'human rights issues,'" it added.
South Korea to co-sponsor the resolution
The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution condemning North Korea's human rights violations every year since 2005.
According to the South Korean Yonhap News Agency, Seoul has decided to co-sponsor the resolution proposed by the EU.
It is the fifth consecutive year that Seoul has done so, following a break from 2019 to 2021 under the liberal Moon Jae-in government.
The draft text is expected to be adopted by the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly later this month, before being submitted to the UN General Assembly for final approval.
