articles.title: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
articles.summary: Easily the most anticipated Bollywood film of the year, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two parts.

blocks.text: India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.

Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.

One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.
Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.

Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka.
Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).

The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.
The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.
But the response so far has been mixed.

Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".
Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars.
"I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.

Shubhra Gupta, external of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".
There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.
Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.

Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King.
"It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote, external, giving it four stars.
Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".

Giovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it, external five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.

The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".

In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.
When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.

Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.
Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.

Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.

The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.

Other adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.
Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters.

It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade-and-a-half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.
The 2023 film Adipurush, another big-budget retelling of Ramayana, sparked backlash on several fronts.

Hindu groups called for a ban, accusing it of disrespecting religious figures, while some critics questioned its depiction of Ravana, which they said drew on Mughal imagery and reinforced stereotypes about Muslims. The film was also criticised for its dialogue and visual effects.
For the actors portraying these characters in the latest film, that burden was deeply felt.
"I was filled with fear," Kapoor told the BBC Asian Network's Haroon Rashid. "I knew that maybe I'm too old for this. I won't be able to do justice to it."
He called the role "an opportunity of a lifetime", but said playing a figure worshipped by millions left little room for the creative freedom he had enjoyed in other films.

Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, said the experience was as much spiritual as artistic. Raised in a religious household, she said she approached the part not just as a performance, but as an opportunity for personal growth.
The film's popular reception will become clearer soon as audiences fill cinemas.
But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale.

articles.title: I thought extra academics made me a good mom. Now I wonder what my daughters lost
articles.summary: Gurpreet Virdi-Bains enrolled her daughters in an after-school math enrichment program to help them get ahead. As she reflects on her own childhood, she considers what it means to be a good parent.

image.caption: Gurpreet Virdi-Bains says pulling her daughters out of an academic enrichment program gave them back their evenings. (Submitted by Gurpreet Virdi-Bains)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person
Gurpreet Virdi-Bains enrolled her daughters in an after-school math enrichment program to help them get ahead. As she reflects on her own childhood, she considers what it means to be a good parent.
I’d forgotten that unstructured time is also a form of learning
· for CBC News
· Posted: Nov 05, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 9 hours ago
This First Person column is the experience of Gurpreet Virdi-Bains, who lives in Caledon, Ont. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

One night, I looked up from wiping down the kitchen counter and noticed how dark it was outside. My daughters' backpacks were still by the door where they always dropped them. The dishwasher hummed in the background, the familiar signal that we were moving toward bedtime. I realized how much of the evening had already slipped by, and we hadn't really been together in it.
It was like this almost every evening.

A few months earlier, I had enrolled my daughters in a math enrichment program. They weren't struggling with math. I enrolled them because I didn't want them to fall behind — because I didn't want to be the parent who left an advantage on the table.
But standing there in the kitchen, I felt what that decision had quietly cost us. Our evenings had become a series of tasks. There was less lingering. Less room to simply exist.

My kids were already spending seven hours in a structured academic environment. Home was supposed to be the break. A craft might get started on a whim, or someone might pick up a book because there was nothing else to do.

items: There’s tired — and then there’s teacher tired. That's me, but it's so worth it

blocks.text: When I think back to my childhood growing up in the 1990s, what stands out most is how little was expected of us after school.

I'm the youngest of three and the daughter of immigrants adjusting to life in a new country. When my two older brothers and I came home from school, we did our homework and then we scattered. Some of us were on the couch, some at the table, the TV humming in the background.
Virdi-Bains, pictured as a two-year-old, grew up in the 1990s. Her parents moved from India to Canada in the 1980s. (Submitted by Gurpreet Virdi-Bains)
We didn't sit down for formal family dinners. Sometimes we ate at different times, half on the sofa, half at the table. No one organized the evening. It simply unfolded.

There were no tutoring or academic enrichment programs waiting for us. We watched Family Matters and Full House. We played outside until it got dark. We read, got bored and figured out what to do next. School stayed at school.
At the time, it felt ordinary. Now I understand how much freedom lived in those evenings.

It wasn't that our parents were absent. They were navigating language and work in a place that still felt new, trying to create something steady for us. We felt safe and cherished in quieter ways — in the routines, in the meals waiting for us, in the expectation that we'd be home before dark.

That didn't mean education was unimportant. It simply looked different. Learning wasn't confined to worksheets or programs. It was woven into everyday life: helping in the kitchen, measuring rice into a pot, shaping roti balls between our palms, counting change at the store, noticing the trees on our walk home and asking questions about them. Nobody called it preparation but it was. We were learning how to look after ourselves.

My parents' version of involvement was sacrifice. It meant long work hours, putting our needs ahead of their own, and doing what they could to keep our lives stable, even if it meant not being present for every moment. They trusted that school would teach us what it needed to, and that we would figure out the rest. Looking back, I see how much faith was embedded in that approach. That kind of separation feels harder to hold onto now.

items: Thinking about joining an extracurricular? Here’s why 2 teens say go for it

blocks.text: I care deeply about education. Before my children started school, I made sure they felt prepared and confident. I practised letters with them at the kitchen table, not as part of a structured plan but in small, unremarkable moments that felt more like play than preparation. We counted steps on the way to the park. I assumed that once school began, learning would mostly stay there, the way it had for me.
Instead, I found myself second-guessing every decision.
Was I doing enough? Should I be doing more?
The pressure crept in through small conversations with other parents. A casual mention at pickup. A program name said in passing. Just enough to linger.

Slowly, I began to believe that being a good parent meant adding more: more structure, more measurable academic progress. Letting evenings unfold started to feel irresponsible, even if my husband didn't fully see it the same way.

items: Kids' math scores are falling. Here's what experts think can fix it.

blocks.text: Writing this column has forced me to admit that some of the pressure wasn't coming from school or other parents. It was coming from me, the daughter of immigrants who doesn't want to squander opportunity. I had internalized the idea that if there was a way to get ahead, you took it, that leaving something on the table — whether it was extra practice, extra support or an added advantage — meant risking falling behind.
After about five months, I withdrew my kids from the program. It was thoughtful and well-run. I understood why families valued it. But I had lost sight of what I wanted our home to feel like.
Virdi-Bains has come to appreciate the value of unstructured time with her daughters. (Submitted by Gurpreet Virdi-Bains)

I still believe deeply in education. What has changed is what I feel compelled to protect: the ordinary moments that make up a childhood. I want my daughters to remember laughter in the kitchen more than the rush from one commitment to the next.

I notice it in small ways. My kids play longer without checking in with me. They ask more questions, even the ones that seem to come out of nowhere at bedtime. When something doesn’t work the first time, they’re more likely to try again on their own before coming to find me. I’d forgotten how much happens in the time I used to think was wasted. That’s often where they figure out what they actually like.

Some evenings, when I notice the light fading earlier than I expected, I remind myself that a free evening doesn’t mean my kids are falling behind. They can play or talk or be bored for a while, and that matters, too.
It's a choice I find myself coming back to again and again.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here’s more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Gurpreet Virdi-Bains is a journalist who writes about parenting and family life.

articles.title: Ramayana: Part 1 has the muscle, but lacks a certain epic soul
articles.summary: Never before has this Hindu myth looked as visually stunning, nor involved so much top-tier talent from across India's and other film industries. But the final effect is mixed.

image.caption: The complex villain Ravana, played by Indian actor Yash, in a scene from Ramayana: Part 1. The two-film adaptation of the Hindu myth is visually impressive and modern but conveys little depth. (Sony Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Never before has this Hindu myth looked as visually stunning, nor involved so much top-tier talent from across India's and other film industries. But the final effect is mixed.
Mega-budget adaptation of Hindu myth feels like it's hurrying you along

Growing up in Toronto, my family got our Indian cinema fix in the late ‘90s by renting bootleg VHS tapes from the basement of a shop on Lawrence Avenue. Usually, that meant fanciful Bollywood romances, but occasionally we'd pick up an episode of an 1987 TV series depicting the ancient Hindu epic poem, the Ramayana.

It was full of telenovela-esque facial reactions, tinfoil jewelry and my favourite: arrows that transformed into other things through the awesome magic of jump cuts. It was appointment viewing for millions of people in India, where it originally aired, and for the diaspora for years to come.

Now, nearly 40 years later, there's the first of two mega-budget adaptations in theatres, Ramayana: Part 1. And despite how visually impressive and modern it is, it's missing the soul found in that melodramatic low-budget TV series.

Believed to have been written several thousand years ago, the Ramayana is a story rooted in Hinduism. But it extends beyond one religion, culture or country. Generally, it's the journey of Prince Rama, a god in human form, as he is drawn into a war with the villainous King Ravana, who abducts the noble princess Sita. The film was directed by Nitesh Tiwari with actors from across Indian cinema — the Hindi-language A-lister Ranbir Kapoor, the Kannada-language star Yash and the Tamil- and Telugu-language actor Sai Pallavi, respectively.
The story's details change across South and Southeast Asia so much that, to quote the scholar A.K. Ramanujan, "one conception [of the story] is quite abhorrent to those who hold another."
And yet the characters are part of everyday life for millions of people, says Aparita Bhandari, an arts and culture reporter in Toronto who grew up in New Delhi.
"You go to the temple, the idea of Ram/Sita, this whole thing is just there in your kind of collective consciousness," she said.
Ranbir Kapoor stars as Prince Rama, a god in human form who is drawn into a war with the villainous Ravana. (Sony Pictures)

Beyond entertainment, the story is full of parables, dealing with struggles and ethics. For example, Prince Rama sacrifices his birthright to be king to his brother, Bharat, and accepts an unfair exile to satisfy his stepmother.
But even with a runtime of over three hours for the Hindi version — and much less for the English dub — some major characters had to be erased or sidelined.
"They had to really cut a whole bunch out of it. You know, like Kaushalya and Sumitra just never spoke," Bhandari said, referring to Rama's birth mother and another stepmother.
Shiv Reddy, a film reviewer who watched both the Hindi and English versions, says the latter even removes a scene with Bharat begging his brother to come back.

A shadow puppet theatre group performs the Ramayana in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Feb. 9, 2025. Southeast Asian cultures have many versions of the myth, which are told in various ways. (Yayuyoshi Chiba/Getty Images/AFP)

"It immensely changed my perception of Ranbir Kapoor's performance as Rama, and also his duty as a king," Reddy told CBC News from Orange, Calif. "And to remove it entirely feels like that conflict that [Rama] faces is removed also."
The end result feels like it's hurrying audiences along, with characters rarely dissecting their motivations, instead telling you something to get you to the next part.
Some glory
And in between that stiff dialogue were often-bombastic action sequences.

From the opening moments, we're greeted with a fantastical battle of angels and demons on an icy battlefield, with war rhinos and a flying elephant battling like Lord of the Rings met God of War and 300.
A flying war elephant arrives on a frigid battlefield in a scene from Ramayana: Part 1. (Sony Pictures)
Loud and crunchy sound design, punctuated by a score from Hans Zimmer, who co-composed it with the equally legendary A.R. Rahman, helped drive these scenes.
For a kid who grew up on that ‘80s series and comic book adaptations, the graphics were impressive (save for a few facial expressions of some demons).
Meeting the moment
The film is timely not just because it's out in theatres for the Diwali weekend — a holiday that celebrates Rama's victory.

It also meets a need for international audiences expecting grand action from the Indian film industry ever since S.S. Rajamouli's RRR in 2022 — and in the process brought together talent from across India and the world to work on both films, which together reportedly cost $500 million US.

items: Nana Patekar, star of Salaam Bombay!, Bollywood films, dead at 75
Beyond Bollywood: RRR and the future of Indian film

blocks.text: Part 1 is playing in more than 50 theatres across this country. Part 2, which has a lot more of the story to cover, has now been delayed to 2028.

"The ambition helped…to tell this grand story," Bhandari said, adding that the money went to a whole wall of artists featured in the end credits. "There's a lot of people that have put a lot of effort into making this work. And I guess to a certain extent, it shows."
But one aspect of the film that some critics feel missed the mark was the use of AI, in post-production, to try to give this story more universal appeal.
In the English dub, which used human voice actors, AI changed the mouths of the actors on-screen to appear as if they were speaking English.
Tiwari, the director, said during the L.A. premiere that this was to "present the film to the world in their language."
For Reddy, it didn't work.
"It's uncanny, for sure," Reddy said. "Because the face is also changing, it feels like it's just not their performance."

Ultimately, AI is an apt analog for this adaptation. Ramayana: Part 1 feels like an AI-generated summary of the ancient epic. You get the gist, you get the polish, but none of the depth until you choose to seek it.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anand Ram is a reporter and producer with CBC's science and climate unit. He's worked as a reporter covering technology, business and the environment and as a producer with The National.

articles.title: 1 in 3 young people in Canada have faced dating violence, pediatricians warn
articles.summary: A third of Canadian youth have faced dating violence — from physical and sexual abuse to online harassment — warns new guidance for health-care providers to help them screen for abusive relationships…

image.caption: New guidance calls on doctors to initiate conversations with young patients about healthy relationships amid an uptick in dating-related violence. (Martin Diotte/CBC)

blocks.text: Health

A third of Canadian youth have faced dating violence — from physical and sexual abuse to online harassment — warns new guidance for health-care providers to help them screen for abusive relationships among kids and teens.
New guidance calls on health-care providers to screen for relationship abuse amid uptick among kids, teens

A third of Canadian youth have faced dating violence — from physical and sexual abuse to online harassment — warns new guidance for health-care providers to help screen for abusive relationships among kids and teens.

Experiencing relationship-based violence at a young age can lead to "both immediate and long-term adverse health outcomes," notes the report, released on Thursday by the Canadian Paediatric Society (CPS). The team defined youth and teens as those in Grade 6 and up, marking the period when dating typically begins.

Health-care providers are seeing an uptick in dating-related violence, said Dr. Megan Harrison, chair of CPS's adolescent health committee, which can range from stalking to psychological abuse to sexual violence and beyond.
3rd of young Canadians aged 11 and up face dating violence, says Canadian Paediatric Society
"And part of that has to do, a little bit, with the increased use of social media and technology for teens," she said.

Violent content that's easily accessible to teens on social media — and in online pornography — is one major part of the problem, echoed Tracy Vaillancourt, a professor at the University of Ottawa and Canada Research Chair in youth mental health and violence prevention.
"It dehumanizes girls and women," she said. "And it's quite problematic to how they see relationships."
Poverty, discrimination increase risk
Multiple researchers also noted that while anyone can fall victim to violence in a romantic or sexual relationship, certain groups are at a higher risk.
Data reported by the CPS shows a higher prevalence of victims among cisgender girls and transgender and gender-diverse youth in a national sample of students in Grades 9 and 10.

items: Experts share advice for kids and teens about abusive relationships

blocks.text: Poverty, marginality and discrimination can also make some youth more vulnerable, noted Dr. Cécile Rousseau, chair of the division of child and adolescent psychiatry at McGill University.

"Sometimes this happens without any explanation, and it's hard to pinpoint why the relationship is violent and abusive, but there's also evidence to suggest that what you've endured in the past predicts what you're willing to endure in the future," Vaillancourt said.
Individuals already experiencing domestic or family violence, or kids who are bullied or rejected by their peer group, are more likely to experience violent relationships as well, she explained.
Experiencing relationship-based violence at a young age can lead to 'both immediate and long-term adverse health outcomes,' researchers said. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
'No easy answer'
So what should doctors — alongside parents and educators — watch out for?

The CPS now recommends that health-care providers, including pediatricians and primary care providers, aim to initiate conversations about healthy relationships during routine medical visits from their young patients, offer privacy and provide community resources as needed.
"Normalizing these discussions at every visit helps build rapport and provides opportunities to share knowledge with youth and caregivers," the guidance notes.

items: As 'Cornell 7' case draws attention, P.E.I. advocates call for better consent education
As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection

blocks.text: But outside experts on dating violence questioned how much health-care providers can do to support teens properly, given the hurdles some young people face in accessing primary care in the first place, and the challenges in linking youth with long-term community support after their visit.

"Studies of adults show that screening for intimate partner violence is only a good thing if you also have resources," Vaillancourt added. "So asking somebody if they're in an unsafe situation and then doing nothing about it is actually quite problematic."

items: Organized crime is using encrypted messaging apps to enlist youth. This spells trouble for police
B.C. Chamber of Commerce delegates reject call for social media, AI ban for kids

blocks.text: Rousseau, from McGill University, said while health-care providers play a "key role" in tackling youth violence, they face an uphill battle given the complexities around why modern teens end up being victims of abuse — or turn to violence themselves.

"Teen dating violence is a problem, but also self-harm, suicide … all of that is increasing very rapidly," said Rousseau, who added the rapid shifts in how teens use technology make it hard for researchers to keep up.
"There is no easy answer," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Pelley is a senior health and medical reporter for CBC News. She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. Contact her at: lauren.pelley@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Will this year’s super El Niño push 2026 to be the warmest year on record?
articles.summary: While the most significant impact on the global temperature typically comes in the months after an El Niño peak — which hasn't happened yet — some climate models are suggesting 2026 could edge out…

image.caption: This map illustrates the temperature anomalies across Earth's oceans. The extreme red in the centre is the current El Niño, with temperatures in some regions reaching as much as 4 C above the average. (Climate Reanalyzer)

blocks.text: Science·New

While the most significant impact on the global temperature typically comes in the months after an El Niño peak — which hasn't happened yet — some climate models are suggesting 2026 could edge out 2024 as the warmest year on record. Could El Niño be influencing this year's global temperature?
Not all climate models suggest 2026 will be the warmest on record
In its monthly temperature update in May, Berkeley Earth, a leading non-profit climate analysis organization, forecast that 2026 had just a 2.5 per cent chance of being the warmest year on record.
Then El Niño started to develop.
The next month it was a 12 per cent chance. By August it had jumped to 69 per cent. Now? Berkeley Earth puts it at a 96 per cent chance.
Is there a link between 2026 potentially being the warmest year on record and this particularly strong El Niño?

This El Niño — a warming in the Pacific Ocean that can contribute to a temporary warming in the global temperature — is already the strongest one since record-keeping began in 1950, beating out the previous record set in 2015-16 by a wide margin.

Scientists consider a strong El Niño to be a warming of 2 C above average. Ocean temperatures in a specific part of the Pacific, near the equator, dubbed “Niño 3.4” reached 3.5 C above average last week.

The ocean temperature in a part of the Pacific Ocean near the equator dubbed Niño 3.4, which is used to measure the strength of an El Niño, is the warmest since records started in 1950. (Climate Central)

Typically, we see the effects of an El Niño on the global temperature about three months after its peak, which is forecast for November or December. However, models show that 2026 will either be the warmest year on record, beating out 2024, or the second-warmest.
“El Niño definitely is leading to the warmth that we're seeing,” said Kent Moore, a professor of atmospheric physics at the University of Toronto.

In its September monthly update, Berkeley Earth reported, "It remains sharply warmer than other months in 2026. September 2026 continued the run of months above the 1.5 C mark that began in July, as the warming influence of El Niño has grown."
But it’s not all El Niño.
Trapped ocean heat

As World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told the Global Heat Forum last month, “El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface.”
And that heat is due to climate change, as we continue to burn fossil fuels, pumping more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

items: 'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'
El Niño is here, and it’s already looking like it could be 'mind-blowing'

blocks.text: “The warmth we're seeing in the ocean ... is mostly related to the fact that we've just been warming the ocean up for the last 150 years,” Moore said.
Overall, global ocean temperatures are the warmest they’ve ever been on record, and that’s because the oceans are really good at trapping excess heat.
Ocean temperatures have been the warmest in recorded history. (Climate Central)
And it turns out they’re also really good at trapping CO2. But there are limits.

“As the ocean warms, the amount of carbon dioxide that it can hold is reduced," said Moore. "So, there's a bit of a feedback loop there. As the oceans warm, they become a less efficient sink for carbon dioxide, which means more of the carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere [and it] warms more.”
I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before
So, while El Niño may be playing a small role in 2026's annual global temperature, the main driver is the use of fossil fuels and greenhouse gases released into our atmosphere.

“You got the slow gradual warming of the ocean, and then the El Niño comes along, kicks [around], for six months or so, [and] the temperature goes way up,” Moore said. “And then, of course, El Niño will go away. But of course the warming will still be there.”
Now, not everyone thinks 2026 will beat out 2024 as the hottest year on record.
The U.S. National Centers for Environmental Information gives only a 0.1 per cent chance of it being the warmest and an 86.9 per cent chance of it being the second-warmest.
But 2027's annual global temperature will definitely be more influenced by El Niño.

Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather, writing for Carbon Brief, a climate publication, said, "This year’s record-setting El Niño will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. Carbon Brief projects 2027 at around 1.7 C above pre-industrial levels, with a 96 per cent chance that it will be the warmest year on record."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Who is Rodil Zalameda, the 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court
articles.summary: Rodil Zalameda is the country's 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court, replacing Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire on November 6.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 4:46pm
Rodil Zalameda is the country's 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court, replacing Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire on November 6.

Before President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. picked him to lead the country's highest tribunal, Zalameda served as an SC associate justice appointed by then-President Rodrigo Duterte on August 6, 2019.
He penned the SC First Division decision, made public on September 9, 2026, overturning the graft conviction of former First Lady Imelda Marcos.
He also penned the SC En Banc decision in 2023 granting a writ of amparo in favor of former Bayan Muna lawmaker Siegfred Deduro.
Zalameda also served as an associate justice of the Court of Appeals from 2008 to 2019 and chairperson of its 17th Division.
He also worked as a city prosecutor and public prosecutor in Mandaluyong City and a branch clerk at the Makati City Regional Trial Court.

The new SC chief justice obtained his Bachelor of Laws degree at Ateneo de Manila University in 1987 under an academic scholarship grant. According to Zalameda's profile posted on the SC website, he was an associate editor of the Ateneo Law Journal, a senior staff member of the Ateneo Law Bulletin, and a member of the Fraternal Order of Utopia.
He passed the Bar examinations in 1988.

He earned his secondary education from the University of the East Caloocan in 1979 and his Bachelor of Arts major in Political Science degree from UE Manila in 1983. UE recently conferred Zalameda the honorary Doctor of Laws degree.
Zalameda was also recognized as one of UE's Outstanding Alumni twice.
In 2006, Zalameda was among the 10 Outstanding Pillars of Justice of the Rotary Club of Diliman.
He also received the Ulirang Mandaleño Award of the Mandaluyong government under the Government Category in 2010.
The Ateneo Law Alumni Association Inc. also bestowed Zalameda the Distinguished Alumni Award under the Judiciary Category in 2022.
Zalameda is born in Caloocan City. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: DA to sustain subsidies, lower tariffs to reduce food supply chain costs
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Thursday it will pursue interventions to slash food supply chain costs as inflation rose to 7.8% in October.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 4:33pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Thursday it will pursue interventions to slash food supply chain costs as inflation rose to 7.8% in October.
The department said it will continue providing fuel and toll subsidies, financial aid, farm inputs, crop insurance, and reduced tariffs on essential animal feed components like corn.
Among the initiatives by the DA is the expansion of the government’s P20 per kilo rice program for the vulnerable sector.

“We are also expanding the coverage of Benteng Bigas, Meron Na!, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s affordable rice program, to help shield vulnerable households, including those with senior citizens, solo parents, and persons with disabilities, from price pressures arising from external shocks beyond the government’s control,” said DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. in a statement.

Food inflation —which tracks the price movements of food items in a “basket” commonly purchased by households— saw a slight decrease of 6.4% from 6.8%, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).
The PSA said the downtrend in food inflation in October was mainly driven by the slower annual increases in the indices of Fish at 5% from 7.4%, and in Vegetables at 5.7% from 10.5%.
Rice remained the largest contributor to overall inflation, while transport and energy costs recorded some of the sharpest increases amid rising fuel prices.
Moreover, Tiu Laurel noted that affordable food depends on a steady supply, warning that climate impacts and geopolitical conflicts continue to jeopardize global and local agricultural production.
“Keeping food prices manageable requires not only bringing down costs but also ensuring that farmers can continue producing enough to meet domestic demand,” the DA said in a statement.

To address price pressures, the Department of Economy, Planning and Development said the government is strengthening agricultural production and logistics while providing targeted assistance to sectors affected by higher energy costs. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Who is Dean Ralph Sarmiento, tapped by Sara Duterte's camp as witness
articles.summary: Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento was listed as Vice President Sara Duterte"s first witness at her impeachment trial. He, however, decided to decline to participate as a witness a day after the…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 3:44pm

Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento was listed as Vice President Sara Duterte’s first witness at her impeachment trial. He, however, decided to decline to participate as a witness a day after the announcement was made.
So who is Sarmiento, and why was he called to become a witness for the Vice President?

On his Facebook profile, Sarmiento listed several educational institutions he attended. In 1992, he received his Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science at University of Negros Occidental – Recoletos.

He earned his Juris Doctor degree at the University of St. La Salle (USLS), where he would spend most of his professional career. Sarmiento graduated Magna Cum Laude from USLS and placed 10th in the 1997 Bar Exams, according to publisher Centralbooks, where the law professor has two books.

In 2002, Sarmiento also studied Classical Works and Scholarly Approaches to the U.S. Constitution as a Fulbright Institute fellow at Temple University in the United States, according to his Facebook profile.
Sarmiento would also go on to study Constitutional and Territorial Reforms in Federal Switzerland as a Swiss Institute of Federalism scholar at the University of Fribourg in 2008.
According to Sarmiento’s LinkedIn page, he has over 28 years of experience working as a law professor at the USLS, where he held various positions.

From June 1998 to May 2010, he was the executive director of the school’s Law Center. From 2010 to 2016, he was the university’s College of Law Dean. He took the position once more from August 2023 to January 2026.

By October 2025, he became the USLS’s Vice Chancellor for Administration. While both his LinkedIn and Facebook profiles still list him as presently working as a vice chancellor, Duterte’s defense team labeled him a “former Vice Chancellor for Administration.”
Sarmiento has over 318,000 followers on Facebook.
During Duterte’s trial, Sarmiento has offered his legal opinions on the matter to several news outlets. Many of his views, however, could also be found online.

“We should hold VP Sara Duterte accountable for every peso of public money and every act properly charged against her. But accountability loses its moral force when fairness is sacrificed. Due process is not a favor to the accused. It is what makes accountability credible,” Sarmiento said in a Facebook post on October 14.

“The Constitution does not ask us to choose between accountability and due process. It demands both, and I support both. I support accountability. I also support due process. We should not have to choose between the two. The stronger the accusation, the greater the need for a complete and tested record,” he added.
The post came a day after the House prosecution dropped three out of the four articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Duterte’s defense team decried the dropping of the cases, as it did not give them a chance to defend the Vice President. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: PH eyes more BrahMos missile units from India, submits wish list -- Teodoro
articles.summary: The Philippines shared a wish list as it plans to acquire additional units of the BrahMos missile system from India, according to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 3:26pm
The Philippines shared a wish list as it plans to acquire additional units of the BrahMos missile system from India, according to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
At the 3rd Delhi Defence Dialogue via video teleconference on Wednesday, Teodoro said the Philippines wants to increase the number of BrahMos units it has acquired from India.

"We hope to increase the number of BrahMos units we have, and we have shared also a wish list on the BrahMos to the Indian authorities in order to make it more tailor-fitted for the Philippine environment," he said.
Teodoro cited logistical challenges in operating and transporting the missile system in the Philippines, including the country's less durable roads and bridges and the absence of an active railroad.
He also pointed out the difficulty of transporting military equipment across the country's more than 7,600 islands.
The Philippines became the first foreign country to acquire the BrahMos missile system from India.

Teodoro said the acquisition is a significant demonstration of India's trust and confidence in the Philippines. According to him, Indian authorities had determined that the country would use the capability responsibly and only for defensive purposes consistent with international law.
In August 2025, President Ferdinand ''Bongbong'' Marcos Jr. said the Philippines is in the process of procuring more BrahMos missiles.
In April 2024, the Indian government confirmed that the first batch of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles was successfully delivered to the Philippines.

Meanwhile, Teodoro identified other potential areas of defense cooperation between the Philippines and Indi including space technology, ground-based air defense systems, multiple-launch rocket systems, and satellite acquisition for the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).
He said Marcos had instructed to pursue an AFP satellite acquisition program with India seen as a potential partner. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: DOTr's Vince Dizon wants review of motorcycle taxi riders cap
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon is looking into reviewing the ceilings on the allowed number of riders on motorcycle-taxi service providers being enforced by the Land Transportation Franchising…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 3:26pm

Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon is looking into reviewing the ceilings on the allowed number of riders on motorcycle-taxi service providers being enforced by the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB).
In a chance interview with reporters, Dizon said, in a mix of Filipino and English, "What I want to understand is what is the current supply and demand situation here in Metro Manila."

"How many passengers are there? How many vehicles are available? It is very clear that there is a scarcity. So this regulation on the… maximum number of riders, I think should be reviewed as I believe that this maximum number if no longer applicable," the Transportation chief said.
"So, it will be discussed with the LTFRB," he said, referring to the motorcycle-taxi rider caps.
Dizon made the pronouncement amid the LTFRB's probe into motorcycle-taxi provider Move It, which was reportedly fined for allegedly exceeding its total authorized limit of 17,746 riders by 55,7575.

In a separate statement, the Coalition of Filipino Commuters (CFC) expressed support to Dizon's pronouncement to review the cap on motorcycle taxi riders and to base regulation on actual commuter demand.

"As the Transport Secretary has pointed out, the current limits were set before the pandemic and no longer reflect conditions on the ground, where public transport in Metro Manila remains scarce. For many commuters, motorcycle taxis are no longer just an alternative," CFC said.

"With Metro Manila generating an estimated 16 million trips a day, according to JICA transport studies, limiting the capacity of these services risks further straining an already overstretched system. Caps do not close the underlying shortage of public transport —they shrink service availability, lengthen waiting times, and leave commuters stranded at the curb with nowhere else to turn," the group said.
CFC said it recognizes that "regulation matters," but it should make these services safer and more accountable, not less accessible.
"Any limit on supply should rest on demonstrable public interest, not on figures that no longer match what commuters need," it said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Speaker Dy backs calls for greater budget transparency
articles.summary: Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Thursday said that Dy said the House of Representatives is open to disclosing supporting documents for government projects and make budget deliberations more…

blocks.text: 'WALANG DAPAT ITAGO'
Published November 5, 2026 2:56pm

Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Thursday said that Dy said the House of Representatives is open to disclosing supporting documents for government projects and make budget deliberations more accessible to the public.
“Walang dapat itago kung walang ginagawang mali. At walang dapat katakutan kung ang layunin ay maglingkod nang tapat,” Dy said.
(There is nothing to hide if nothing wrong is being done. And there is nothing to fear if the intention is to serve honestly.)
“Ang badyet ay pera ng taumbayan. Karapatan nilang malaman kung paano ito ginagastos,” he added.
(The budget is the people's money. It is their right to know how it is being spent.)

The People’s Budget Coalition has flagged P170 billion increase in budget for multi-purpose buildings and local road projects. It also flagged eight farm to market roads with locations mapped in seas.
The Department of Agriculture has since clarified that the eight farm to market locations with wrong coordinates were a typographical error on its part.
Dy, meanwhile, said that amendments introduced by lawmakers in the P7.2 trillion proposed budget should not be presumed "anomalous."

“Hindi lahat ng pagbabagong ginagawa ng Kongreso sa badyet ay mali. Tungkulin ng mga kongresista na ipaglaban ang pangangailangan ng kanilang mga distrito. Ang mahalaga, maayos ang proyekto, kumpleto ang dokumento at may tunay na pakinabang sa tao,” Dy said.

(Legitimate congressional amendments should not automatically be associated with corruption. What is important here is that the projects are backed up with documents and would be of service to the community.)
The Speaker also expressed support for reforms that would make government assistance more accessible based on people’s needs rather than political connections.

“The House is prepared to work with the Senate, executive agencies and civil society organizations to ensure that public funds address urgent national concerns, including food security, healthcare, education, employment, infrastructure and preparations for El Niño,” he added.
The House has already approved the proposed P7.2 trillion budget on third and final reading.
The Senate is still deliberating on the proposed 2027 national budget.

articles.title: SSS partners with DICT to integrate digital ID into eGov app
articles.summary: The Social Security System (SSS) has partnered with the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) to integrate the MySSS Card's digital ID feature and select member services into…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 2:51pm

The Social Security System (SSS) has partnered with the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) to integrate the MySSS Card's digital ID feature and select member services into the eGovPH app.
The partnership was forged through a data-sharing agreement signed on October 21, 2026, in Quezon City by DICT Secretary Robert Joseph de Claro and SSS President and CEO Victor Alfonso Limlingan.
The partnership came shortly after de Claro's appointment as DICT Secretary, following his tenure as SSS chief.

"This partnership marks a major step in making SSS services more accessible and convenient for our members. By integrating the digital MySSS Card and key services into the eGovPH superapp, we are bringing social security closer to every Filipino—right at their fingertips," said Limlingan.
Once integrated, the SSS said its members will be able to access the front-facing digital representation of their MySSS Card as one of the IDs available through the eGovPH superapp.
Members will also be able to view their contribution history, total number of contributions, latest membership type, and most recent employer information.

"Our members should not have to visit multiple offices or use multiple applications just to access basic services. Through eGovPH superapp, we are making it easier for Filipinos to check their contributions, verify their membership status, and access their MySSS Card—all in one place," said Limlingan.

"We are proud to be part of this national effort to unify government services. The SSS remains committed to leveraging technology to deliver faster, more secure, and more member-centered service," added the SSS chief. — VDV, GMA News

November 5, 2026
Overall deportations down, but returns to Turkey on the rise

The number of people deported from Germany decreased by nearly 19% from January to September 2026 compared to the previous year, the Interior Ministry announced following a request from the Left Party.
Some 14,324 people were deported in the first nine months of this year, down from 17,651 in 2025. Turkey was the most common destination, followed by Georgia and Algeria.
The numbers reveal that deportations to Syria remain difficult due to the political situation there, even for convicted criminals. Six people have been returned there since the beginning of 2026.
Deportations to Turkey, however, appeared to buck the trend, as 2,025 people have been sent there.

According to the Interior Ministry, the number of foreign nationals leaving the country voluntarily has also slightly increased. Some 14,140 people have received assistance to return to their countries of origin, compared to 12,263 the year before.

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats eye historic upset in Mississippi Senate race as Republican blame game begins
articles.summary: Democrat Scott Colom is leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the southern state; JD Vance pointed to the war in Iran as the ‘obvious’ culprit for Republicans’ loss

blocks.text: Mississippi count continues with Democratic candidate ahead by a razor-thin margin
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the 2026 midterms where almost 24 hours after Democrats secured their historic sweep of the US Congress, two Senate seats remain in play.

Counting in Alaska is expected to continue into Thursday, while in deep red Mississippi, Democrats could be close to pulling off another almighty upset. Currently, Democrat Scott Colom is leading his Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,138 votes with almost 96% of the vote counted.
In the last few hours, votes for Colom have been outpacing those for his Republican opponent, although new batches of votes have not been reported for several hours now.
Although a race this close would automatically trigger a recount in some states, Mississippi has no law on the books for initiating a recount.

blocks.caption: Mississippi Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom on Wednesday.  Photograph: Sue Dorfman/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Democrats haven’t won a US Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, and Donald Trump carried the state by 22 points in 2024. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state elected a Black person to that office.

Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friends with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician. In 2015, he unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions.
Meanwhile, after Democrats secured their historic wins in last night’s midterm elections, Republicans are beginning the blame game:

items: Donald Trump claimed Republicans fared poorly because he was not on the ballot – after repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot.
JD Vance pointed to Trump’s ongoing war in Iran as the “obvious” culprit for the loss.

Pete Hegseth’s role leading the unpopular war could lead to him taking the fall – despite Trump publicly backing him. Republicans including Trump foe Thomas Massie have criticized the defense secretary.

Ron DeSantis, Florida’s governor, said the “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” was caused in part by his party failing to target their ad spending on issues that would motivate voters.

blocks.text: According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. But how will Trump cope with this new political reality?
The Guardian’s David Smith explores that – and whether these elections mark the beginning of the end for Trump – this analysis piece here:

articles.title: ‘Bring it on’: Pauline Hanson to appeal Mehreen Faruqi racial discrimination ruling in high court
articles.summary:
One Nation leader granted special leave to appeal after full federal court earlier this year agreed Hanson portrayed Faruqi as a ‘second-class citizen’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s high court has agreed to hear Pauline Hanson’s appeal against a ruling that she engaged in racial discrimination against Mehreen Faruqi when she told the Greens senator to “pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan”.
The One Nation leader was granted special leave to appeal on Thursday after the full federal court earlier this year unanimously upheld a 2024 decision.
The high court will examine whether Hanson’s comments breached the Racial Discrimination Act (RDA) or if the federal court decision impeded her implied freedom of speech.
Hanson welcomed the decision on social media, saying “this case has always been bigger than me and bigger than one tweet”.
“Australians must be able to speak their minds, question their government and disagree with each other without being frightened into silence,” the 72-year-old senator wrote.
“That freedom is under attack, including through Labor’s digital duty of care bill and its threat to lawful debate online.”
Faruqi said in a statement on Thursday: “Bring it on.”
“This has been a long, hard road walked alongside everyone who has been targeted by racism. We won’t be backing down now,” the Greens senator wrote.

“The highest court in Australia can now determine once and for all that people in this country are protected against racism. People of colour, migrants and Muslims deserve to feel safe in the place they call home. In times like these where we are being attacked and demonised, our legal system must be able to provide protection against vilification.”
A spokesperson for the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said section 18C of the RDA was more important to Australia’s social cohesion “than ever”.

“As the matter is before the court, it would be inappropriate to comment further,” the spokesperson said. “The Australian government’s position is clear: there is no place for racism or racial hatred in our society.”
The dispute arose in 2022 after the death of Queen Elizabeth II.
after newsletter promotion

Faruqi tweeted: “Condolences to those who knew the Queen. I cannot mourn the leader of a racist empire built on stolen lives, land and wealth of colonised peoples. We are reminded of the urgency of Treaty with First Nations, justice & reparations for British colonies & becoming a republic.”

In response, Hanson posted: “Your attitude appalls and disgusts me. When you immigrated to Australia you took every advantage of this country. You took citizenship, bought multiple homes, and a job in a parliament. It’s clear you’re not happy, so pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan – PH.”

Justice Angus Stewart in November 2024 found Hanson’s tweet was unlawful and portrayed Faruqi as a “second-class citizen” who took advantage of Australia and who, as a migrant to the country, “should be grateful for what she has and keep quiet” – a position he declared to be “exclusionary”.

Stewart found Hanson’s comment that Faruqi should “piss off back to Pakistan” was a “variant of the slogan ‘go back to from where you came from’”, which he said was a “racist trope” and a “strong form of racism”. He added that Hanson’s tweet, given her profile, likely “empowered others” to make similar or worse comments.

The judge rejected Hanson’s arguments, including that Faruqi’s tweet on the queen’s death justified her response. He found Hanson’s tweet did not fall within the fair comment exemption because it was an “angry, personal attack”.
Stewart’s judgment was unanimously upheld in July this year by the three federal court judges Melissa Perry, Geoffrey Kennett and Elizabeth Bennett.

articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.summary:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials…

blocks.text: The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
after newsletter promotion
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.

“Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

articles.title: Protesters to join nationwide march as France braces for day of strike action
articles.summary:
Hospital workers, air traffic and rail staff expected to join strikes amid renewed protests over education and rising living costs

Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in…

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.

President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office continue to be marred by domestic crises, as high school students protesting over poor teaching conditions have been joined by workers in weekly protests over the cost of living. Meanwhile, the government is struggling to pass a belt-tightening budget in a divided parliament as public debt approaches 120% of economic output.

Ahead of Thursday’s strike action, France’s four main rail unions said that the government’s proposed budget cuts would “worsen poverty, slash social security, freeze state workers’ salaries and dry up investment needed for environmental measures”.

Amid the renewed protests centred on living costs, public spending cuts and the troubled education system, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate Marine Le Pen is polling high for the 2027 presidential election to replace Macron next spring.

High school students continued to blockade schools over overcrowded classes and dilapidated buildings, saying the government’s proposed measures on capping some class sizes and loaning funds to regional authorities to fix schools were not enough. University students joined in blockading some faculties. Trade unions from across the political landscape joined in a call for strikes over the rising cost of living, with private schools’ teachers unions also joining strikes alongside state school teachers.

blocks.caption: French soldiers patrol a street in Paris on the eve of the strikes. Rights’ groups objected to the ‘authoritarian’ attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: Rights’ groups protested over what they said was heavy policing and an “authoritarian” attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate.

The French Human Rights League said there was an “authoritarian shift” to stifle “any dissenting voice” as the government put in place heavy policing and authorities issued restrictions on demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in certain areas.

Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “We’re living at a very serious time with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government”, criticising decisions by authorities in cities such as Rennes, Toulouse and Lyon to push demonstrations out of city centres.
after newsletter promotion
Marylise Léon, the head of the moderate CFDT trade union, said: “The principle of a demonstration is its visibility.”

The national rail operator SNCF said there would be “disturbances” to train services on regional lines and some parts of the greater Paris area. Dockers said there would be disruption in French ports. The education ministry said it expected almost 18% of nursery and primary school teachers to strike. Trade unions said they also expected secondary teachers to take part in Thursday’s strike.

articles.title: South Korea says it will expand naval operations closer to strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Seoul to seek parliamentary approval to extend anti-piracy Cheonghae unit’s area to about 650km from the vital strait after criticism from Donald Trump on Iran war support

South Korea plans…

blocks.text: South Korea plans to expand the operations ⁠of its anti-piracy unit to waters closer to the strait of Hormuz, its defence ministry has said, after pressure from Donald Trump to ⁠provide support for his war in Iran.

The government is to submit a motion to parliament that would expand the Cheonghae unit’s area of operation to waters near the port of Duqm in Oman, which ​is about 650km (403 miles) away from the strait. The motion also needs to be approved by ‌President Lee Jae Myung and the cabinet.
“The enhancement of the Cheonghae unit’s mission is to protect our citizens and safeguard our economic interests,” a defence ministry official told reporters.
The reinforcement was strictly for non-combat purposes and the unit would operate independently of allied forces, said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“Operations will remain restricted to the open waters south of Oman, and the maritime patrol aircraft will be prohibited from targeting or monitoring Iranian territory, territorial waters or the interior of the strait of Hormuz during their missions,” he said.

Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint ⁠military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that ​unsettled the US ally.
The unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009 to ensure safe navigation of commercial vessels.
The motion also seeks to ​extend the unit’s deployment to the Middle ‌East, which is set ‌to expire at the end of 2026, a ministry spokesperson said, confirming a report by Yonhap ‌news agency.
It currently includes a 4,400-ton-class destroyer, a maritime operations helicopter, up to three rigid-hull inflatable boats and about 300 service members, according to broadcaster YTN.
Seoul would also deploy a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and increase the unit’s personnel by 75, the Korea Herald reported.
South ​Korea relies heavily on oil ​imports and sourced 70% of its supplies from the Middle East in ​2025, most of ‌it delivered through the ​strait of Hormuz, ​according to the industry ministry.

Lee said on 18 September that he would not deploy military assets to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict, but that Seoul was reviewing playing a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
articles.summary: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.

blocks.text: Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, says she is "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict.

"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC.
Human Rights Watch described the ruling as "cruel and unjust".

"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.

The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also for colluding with foreign forces.
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.

However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.

By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.

Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.

Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.

On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."
Additional reporting by Martin Yip

articles.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
articles.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.

blocks.text: With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?
By
Washington correspondent

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

blocks.caption: JD Vance walks on a stage. An American flag is behind him

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.
